\chapter{Describing Things}
\label{ch:sa-describing-things}
\hlchaptermodality{15}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at something in Sanskrit and ask who or where it is — and I can say what the six words have in common.}

Say the near word, the far word and the question word in a row, and name the part that changed.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mahat]{\sk{महत्} (mahat) — big}

\label{lesson:SA-C15-big}



\begin{quote}
You can already name things. This is how you POINT at them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{महत्}}
\textbf{\sk{महत्}} — \emph{mahat} — big.

Put it in front of a word you already know and you have said something new. That is all an adjective does in this language.

The last lesson of this chapter gives the one rule that governs every adjective you will ever meet here.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\sk{महत्}\textquotedblright{} three times, pointing at something different each time
  \item it once with a word you already know after it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{mahat}? (\textbf{big}.) Where does it go — before the word it describes, or after? (\textbf{Before.})
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[before the noun, and it AGREES]{before the noun, and it AGREES — five words, one rule}

\label{lesson:SA-C15-adjective-system}



\begin{quote}
Say the five words from this chapter out loud, then say each one in front of a noun you already know.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: where an adjective goes}]
You did not learn five separate words. You learned \textbf{where an adjective goes}, and five words that go there.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{meaning} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
big & \textbf{\sk{महत्}} \emph{mahat} \\
small & \textbf{\sk{अल्प}} \emph{alpa} \\
good & \textbf{\sk{उत्तम}} \emph{uttama} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Sanskrit agrees too, and in more ways than Hindi does — this is where Hindi's habit comes from.

This is worth more than the five words are. Every noun you already know — your name, the house, the water, the day — can now take any of them in front, and every adjective you meet from here goes in the same place.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} each of the five in front of a noun you already know
  \item \emph{Say it:} two of them with the same noun, one after the other
  \item \emph{Notice:} whether the adjective changed shape when the noun did
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does an adjective go in this language? (\textbf{In front of the noun.}) Does it change shape to match the noun? (and it AGREES.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ha]{\sk{ह} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S114-letter-ha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \sk{प} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ह}}
\textbf{\sk{ह}} — \emph{ha}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{h}, it is \textbf{ha}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a descending right stem joined to the leftward shoulder and clockwise hooked body
  \item a separate down-right outer curve and tail
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{ह} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{अहम्}} \emph{aham} — I
  \item \textbf{\sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि}} \emph{ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi} — I speak Sanskrit
  \item \textbf{\sk{गृह्णाति}} \emph{gṛhṇāti} — he, she, or it takes, seizes
  \item \textbf{\sk{साहाय्यं} \sk{करोति}} \emph{sāhāyyaṁ karoti} — he, she, or it helps
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ह}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the right stem's headline junction, descend, sweep left through the shoulder, then curve clockwise around the hooked body to its lower-right tip without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at the body's left junction and sweep down-left around the outer curve, then continue diagonally down-right through the tail
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified three-stroke teaching form; the corroborating deskbook stages the joined first body in more component steps.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{ह}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 9 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \sk{ह} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{अहम्}  ·  \sk{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ह} three times, saying \emph{ha} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{ह} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{ह}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ha}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
